thema_eingabe: Claude Code: You're Using Claude Code Wrong: Do This Instead

teile.name: Wrong problem
teile.text: Is Claude Code solving the wrong problem? It reads files and runs commands. Jumping straight to code can miss the point.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: black-haired man in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses rubs his forehead at a cluttered night desk, city lights behind him, medium shot, moody blue lighting.

teile.name: Plan mode
teile.text: Anthropic's guide says start in plan mode. Press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows plan mode on. Claude reads without changes.
teile.szene: Painted urban game-poster style close shot of the cyan-glasses presenter's hands pressing two keys on a keyboard, neon reflections on his glasses, dim studio loft, calm space above and below.

teile.name: Ask for a plan
teile.text: Ask for a plan. The guide's example: add Google OAuth, which files change? Ctrl+G opens the plan in your editor.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game style: the cyan-glasses presenter leans back in a rooftop workspace, thoughtful expression, hand on chin, city skyline at dusk, medium shot, warm orange rim light.

teile.name: Code and test
teile.text: Then approve the plan and let Claude code. The guide suggests asking for tests, running the suite, and fixing failures.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in black leather jacket and cyan glasses gives a confident nod while sitting at a street-level cafe table, rainy evening, medium shot, glowing reflections.

teile.name: Context limit
teile.text: So why does this matter? Context fills fast, and performance degrades as it fills. Claude may forget earlier instructions.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses presenter watches a crowded room with stacked boxes piling to the ceiling around him, puzzled look, wide shot, dramatic side lighting.

teile.name: Small fixes and checks
teile.text: Plan mode adds overhead for small fixes. For bigger work, plan first, so Claude solves the right problem. Then give it a test.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in cyan glasses smiles with relief, arms crossed, standing on a sunlit balcony above a lively city street, medium shot, warm light.

teile.name: Abschluss
teile.text: Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses presenter gives a friendly thumbs up at a neon-lit city corner at night, medium close shot, calm space above and below.

regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Match every spoken reference to tool actions, UI elements, or code changes with on-screen visuals showing exact genuine source-supported code editors, compiler outputs, or benchmark diagrams.
Each visual change must introduce a materially different subject, action, or tool example; simple zooms, crops, label swaps, text graphics, or repeated presenter poses do not count as new motifs.
Never use plain text overlays, bullet points, or title cards that merely repeat the spoken narration as a substitute for real tool interfaces, code, or benchmark visuals.
Place the mandatory spoken CTA (like, share, save) at the format-specific position prescribed for Shorts or long videos; do not substitute other calls-to-action.
Open with a user-focused hook that states the practical human task the tool solves, avoiding abstract architecture, benchmark, or parameter details.
Provide concrete proof for any claimed benefit (e.g., installation commands, terminal logs, clickable UI buttons, authentic output screenshots, or benchmark diagrams).
Respect format-specific pacing: do not apply long-video chapter pacing to Shorts, and do not impose Shorts-style rapid speed on long-form content.
Treat reviewer feedback as provisional data: apply observable, concrete fixes to the indicated segments without over-generalising a single defect into a style ban.
Never override source-supported facts, limits, or approved voices; factual accuracy and source citation take precedence over creative choices.
When narration mentions a specific example or UI interaction, insert a matching concrete visual example (real webpage, specific button state, or interaction demo).
Preserve the channel's visual identity: use the black-haired presenter with cyan glasses, original painted open-world-game style backgrounds, and avoid unrelated stock or fictional characters.

If a visual element is missing or mismatched, replace it with a genuine, source-backed screenshot or diagram that directly demonstrates the spoken point (e.g., code editor, decoder output, benchmark chart).

schwaechen: Sentence: 'It reads files and runs commands.' Why it matters: This generic descriptive statement immediately stalls the hook's momentum instead of clarifying why jumping straight into code causes Claude Code to fail. Feasible fix: Cut the description and merge the opening into a direct causal risk: 'When you let Claude Code jump straight to code, it often solves the wrong problem.'

Sentence: 'So why does this matter? Context fills fast, and performance degrades as it fills.' Why it matters: Delaying the technical reason—context degradation—until after the step-by-step UI instructions leaves the viewer following arbitrary menu steps without understanding the underlying stakes. Feasible fix: Move the context degradation rationale right behind the introduction of plan mode so the viewer understands why Claude must read without making changes before they learn the shortcuts.

hooklabor.alt: Is Claude Code solving the wrong problem?
kandidaten: Claude Code can read your files and run commands.
Most people let Claude Code write code before it understands anything.
You press Shift+Tab, and Claude Code stops changing your files.
What if Claude Code could read everything but change nothing?
Claude Code just solved the right problem, and here's how.

belege.text:
Official Claude Code documentation/help page.
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Best practices for Claude Code - Claude Code Docs
Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt
Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
Claude Code is an agentic coding environment. Unlike a chatbot that answers questions and waits, Claude Code can read your files, run commands, make changes, and autonomously work through problems while you watch, redirect, or step away entirely.
This changes how you work. Instead of writing code yourself and asking Claude to review it, you describe what you want and Claude figures out how to build it. Claude explores, plans, and implements.
But this autonomy still comes with a learning curve. Claude works within certain constraints you need to understand.
This guide covers patterns that have proven effective across Anthropic’s internal teams and for engineers using Claude Code across various codebases, languages, and environments. For how the agentic loop works, see How Claude Code works .
Most best practices are based on one constraint: Claude’s context window fills up fast, and performance degrades as it fills.
Claude’s context window holds your entire conversation, including every message, every file Claude reads, and every command output. However, this can fill up fast. A single debugging session or codebase exploration might generate and consume tens of thousands of tokens.
This matters since LLM performance degrades as context fills. When the context window is getting full, Claude may start “forgetting” earlier instructions or making more mistakes. The context window is the most important resource to manage. To see how a session fills up in practice, watch an interactive walkthrough of what loads at startup and what each file read costs. Track context usage continuously with a custom status line , and see Reduce token usage for strategies on reducing token usage.
Give Claude a way to verify its work
Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare. It’s the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from.
Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, “looks done” is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop: every mistake waits for you to notice it. Give Claude something that produces a pass or fail, and the loop closes on its own. Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and iterates until the check passes.
The check is anything that returns a signal Claude can read in the conversation: a test suite, a build exit code, a linter, a script that diffs output against a fixture, or a browser screenshot compared against a design. Run /verify yourself after Claude’s check passes to confirm the change against the running app.
Provide verification criteria ”implement a function that validates email addresses" "write a validateEmail function. example test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. run the tests after implementing”
Verify UI changes visually ”make the dashboard look better" "[paste screenshot] implement this design. take a screenshot of the result and compare it to the original. list differences and fix them”
Address root causes, not symptoms ”the build is failing" "the build fails with this error: [paste error]. fix it and verify the build succeeds. address the root cause, don’t suppress the error”
Once the check exists, decide how hard it gates the stop:
In one prompt : ask Claude to run the check and iterate in the same message, as in the table above.
Across a session : set the check as a /goal condition . A separate evaluator re-checks it after every turn and Claude keeps working until the goal resolves. If Claude stalls, Claude Code eventually stops the run with the goal still set — see how /goal evaluation works .
As a deterministic gate : a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. Stop input covers the cap on consecutive blocks.
By a second opinion : a verification subagent or a dynamic workflow that checks its own findings has a fresh model try to refute the result, so the agent doing the work isn’t the one grading it.
Each step trades setup for attention. The prompt version works on any task today. The /goal and Stop hook versions are what let an unattended run finish correctly without you.
Have Claude show evidence rather than asserting success: the test output, the command it ran and what it returned, or a screenshot of the result. Reviewing evidence is faster than re-running the verification yourself, and it works for sessions you weren’t watching.
Explore first, then plan, then code
Separate research and planning from implementation to avoid solving the wrong problem.
Letting Claude jump straight to coding can produce code that solves the wrong problem. Use plan mode to separate exploration from execution.
The recommended workflow has four phases:
Enter plan mode by pressing Shift+Tab until the status bar shows ⏸ plan mode on , or start the session with claude --permission-mode plan . Claude reads files and answers questions without making changes.
read /src/auth and understand how we handle sessions and login.
also look at how we manage environment variables for secrets.
Ask Claude to create a detailed implementation plan.
I want to add Google OAuth. What files need to change?
What's the session flow? Create a plan.
Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor for direct editing before Claude proceeds.
Switch out of plan mode by approving the plan or pressing Shift+Tab , then let Claude code, verifying against its plan.
implement the OAuth flow from your plan. write tests for the
callback handler, run the test suite and fix any failures.
Ask Claude to commit with a descriptive message and create a PR.
commit with a descriptive message and open a PR
